Subject: Request: isolation pattern + SOC 2 / SIG evidence for Dedicated & Private

Hi Priya,

Thanks for taking this. We are preparing our control mapping for an upcoming SOC 2 intake and need a concise architecture narrative + evidence bundle for your Dedicated and Private deployment options. Specifically Globex is focused on:

- The logical "airlock" pattern you run for customer ingress/egress between customer VPC and Redwood-managed compute (diagram + narrative)
- Tenant fencing controls (how you prevent cross-customer KV cache / memory leakage)
- Egress controls and approved destination lists, and how you attest they are enforced for Private deployments
- A short list of artifacts we can reference in SIG / CAIQ answers (diagrams, policy docs, sample audit logs)

Can you send a one-page overview and any attachments you can share? Our compliance window is the week of Dec 7.

Cheers,
Elena

Subject: Re: Request: isolation pattern + SOC 2 / SIG evidence for Dedicated & Private

Elena,

Appreciate the heads-up. Attaching a short narrative and three artifacts that map directly to SIG/CAIQ controls: an airlock topology PNG, an egress policy matrix spreadsheet, and a tenant fencing readme. High-level summary below and I’ve highlighted where to cite each artifact in the CAIQ: 

Summary (TL;DR):
- Airlock topology: Dedicated deployments place a small customer-configured ingress VPC peering (or PrivateLink) to a dedicated edge plane. Traffic enters a hardened edge fleet (TLS termination, WAF, minimal host surface) and is proxied to dedicated GPU pools via service mesh tunnels. The attached PNG (airlock-topology-v1.png) shows the logical zones and control points.
- Tenant fencing: We use per-deployment GPU pools and per-model process isolation. Runtime enforces strict KV cache namespaces and ephemeral allocation; cross-tenant memory sharing is prevented by kernel-level allocator boundaries and conservative sharing flags. See tenant-fencing-readme.pdf for the runtime attestations and sample trace that shows allocation boundaries.
- Egress controls: For Private deployments, egress is controlled via a managed egress gateway that enforces allow-lists, TLS deep-inspection hooks (customer-controlled), and DNS policy. The egress-policy-matrix.xlsx lists approved destination categories, default blocks, and audit events that map to SIG control TM-1/TM-2.

What I’ve attached (redacted where necessary):
- airlock-topology-v1.png (logical diagram, public network removed)
- egress-policy-matrix.xlsx (catalog of allowed destinations + audit signal columns)
- tenant-fencing-readme.pdf (runtime fencing narrative + sample logs)

Next steps: If you want a short recorded walkthrough, Marissa can record a 10-minute call showing the diagram and pointing at the logs. Karthik is on standby for deeper questions about kernel-level isolation and the SOC 2 mapping.

I’ll also drop a short writeup linking each artifact to relevant SIG/CAIQ questions (will send by EOD tomorrow).

Thanks,
Priya

Thanks Priya — quick review looks promising. Two quick clarifications before we hand this to our audit team: 

1) For the tenant fencing readme, can you confirm whether the sample logs include request IDs that correlate across the edge and compute layers (we need an ability to trace an individual inference request end-to-end)?
2) For Private (VPC) deployments, are customers able to provide their own egress allow-lists, or does Redwood enforce the default? We need language to cite that the customer remains in control of permitted destinations.

If those are straightforward I can fold them into the CAIQ answers. If not, we may need a 20-min call with Karthik. Appreciate the quick turnaround.

—Elena

From: Priya Natarajan <priya_natarajan@redwood.com>
To: Elena Cruz <elena.cruz@globex.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-12-02T14:05:00-05:00
Subject: Re: Request: isolation pattern + SOC 2 / SIG evidence for Dedicated & Private

Elena,

Short answers below and we can expand in a follow-up note/call.

1) Traceability: Yes — our edge inserts a per-request canonical ID (x-rw-request-id) at TLS termination and that ID is propagated through the service mesh to the compute plane. tenant-fencing-readme.pdf contains an example trace showing the ID across the edge, proxy, and GPU-worker logs. The sample logs have been redacted for customer PII but preserve the request IDs you can use for trace correlation.

2) Egress control model for Private deployments: Customers may supply a custom allow-list managed by their admin (via the Redwood Admin UI or API) — by default we ship a conservative-deny baseline that customers must opt to relax. Enforcement is done at the managed egress gateway in the customer VPC; audit logs and per-destination flow records are available for 90 days (longer retention available as an add-on).

If helpful, Karthik and I can join a 20-minute call Thursday (Dec 8) to walk your audit team through the artifacts and show the trace snippet live. Marissa will book if you confirm a time.

Best,
Priya

--
Priya Natarajan
